blocks.content: The manifest structure introduced two topics ago showed paths mapped to backends without lingering on the mechanism. This topic gives that mechanism, one of the two pillars every Ingress rule is built from, its full dedicated depth.
Path Based Routing, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Path Based Routing, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Path based routing is the Ingress mechanism that directs a request to a specific backend Service based on the URL path the request is targeting, letting one hostname serve many genuinely distinct applications underneath it.

A request to example.com slash api and a request to example.com slash app share the exact same hostname but can be routed to two entirely different backend Services, each unaware of the other's existence.

This is expressed in an Ingress manifest through the path field within each rule's paths array, combined with a pathType value that determines exactly how that path string is matched against incoming requests.

Path based routing is the single most common mechanism used to consolidate multiple application components behind one domain name, and it is frequently the very first Ingress capability a new team reaches for in practice.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643060109-642129090.png
blocks.alt: Path based routing given its own full depth

blocks.content: How Path Prefix Matching Actually Works
blocks.text: How Path Prefix Matching Actually Works

blocks.content: The most common pathType value, Prefix, matches any request whose URL begins with the specified path, meaning a rule for slash api matches slash api, slash api slash users, and slash api slash orders slash 123 all identically.

A second pathType value, Exact, matches only the precise path given, with no partial or prefix matching at all, useful for narrowly scoped rules where accidental over matching would be a genuine problem.

When multiple rules could plausibly match the same incoming request, the Ingress controller applies the most specific matching rule, meaning a longer, more precise path prefix takes priority over a shorter, more general one.

Understanding this prefix matching behavior precisely, rather than assuming exact string equality, is essential for correctly predicting how a given Ingress manifest will actually route real, varied incoming traffic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643062081-290972953.png
A Real Path Based Routing Example
blocks.text: A Real Path Based Routing Example

blocks.content: Consider a single domain, example.com, serving both a REST API and a web application frontend, with the API team and the frontend team each owning and deploying their own Service entirely independently of one another.

An Ingress rule for the api path prefix routes to the api-service Service, while a separate rule for the app path prefix routes to the frontend-service Service, both defined under the exact same host within one Ingress object.

A user visiting example.com slash app slash dashboard is transparently routed to the frontend Service, while a request to example.com slash api slash users is routed to the entirely separate API Service, both from the exact same public domain.

Neither backend Service needs to know anything about the other, and either one can be scaled, updated, or replaced independently, with the Ingress rule as the sole, centralized place where the actual routing decision is made.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: example-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /app
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: frontend-service
                port:
                  number: 80

blocks.content: Recap: HTTP Aware Routing, Now Concrete
blocks.text: Recap: HTTP Aware Routing, Now Concrete

blocks.content: The very first topic in this module introduced HTTP aware routing as the core capability separating Ingress from every Service type, describing it in general terms without yet showing exactly how such a rule is written.

Path based routing is the first of the two concrete mechanisms that fulfill that earlier description, giving actual, working shape to what was previously an abstract claim about routing by request content rather than by raw connection alone.

Seeing an actual working manifest, exactly as shown in this topic's real example, should make that earlier, more abstract description click into place as something genuinely concrete and immediately usable, not just a conceptual promise.

Host based routing, covered in the very next topic, completes this picture as the second of the two mechanisms, and together the two form the complete routing vocabulary nearly every real Ingress manifest is built from.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643065261-190030145.png
blocks.alt: Recap of what is Ingress, now made concrete

blocks.content: Rewriting the Path Before Forwarding

By default, the Ingress controller forwards the full original path to the backend Service, meaning a request to slash api slash users arrives at the API Service still carrying that full slash api prefix in its own path.

Many backend applications are written without any awareness of the slash api prefix, expecting requests to simply arrive at slash users directly, which creates a mismatch unless the prefix is deliberately stripped somewhere along the way.

Most Ingress controller implementations support a rewrite target annotation, instructing the controller to strip the matched prefix before forwarding the request, letting the backend application remain genuinely unaware of the path prefix used to route to it externally.

This rewrite capability is a small but genuinely important detail that determines whether backend applications need to be written with Ingress specific path awareness baked in, or whether they can remain simple and portable regardless of how they are externally routed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643066949-303752468.png
blocks.alt: A path rewrite annotation stripping the prefix before forwarding

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Incorrect Rule Ordering
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Incorrect Rule Ordering

blocks.content: A common mistake is defining overlapping path prefixes within a single Ingress object in an order that causes a more general rule to unintentionally shadow a more specific one, capturing traffic that was meant to reach a different backend entirely.

For example, a rule for the bare slash path defined carelessly can unintentionally match every single request, including ones meant for slash api, if the Ingress controller's specific implementation does not apply the most specific match rule as expected.

While most modern Ingress controllers correctly prioritize more specific paths automatically, relying on this implicit behavior without testing it explicitly is a fragile habit that can behave differently across different controller implementations.

The safer, more explicit practice is ordering rules from most specific to least specific within the manifest itself, and testing the actual resulting routing behavior directly rather than assuming a particular priority behavior silently holds.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643068661-534700150.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of ordering overlapping path rules incorrectly

blocks.content: Path Based Routing Across Multiple Ingress Objects
blocks.text: Path Based Routing Across Multiple Ingress Objects

blocks.content: Rules for the same host can be split across multiple separate Ingress objects rather than consolidated into one, which is a common pattern in larger organizations where different teams own and deploy their own Ingress manifests independently.

The Ingress controller merges rules from every Ingress object targeting the same host automatically, meaning a team can add a new path prefix for their own application without needing to edit a shared, centrally owned Ingress manifest at all.

This decentralized ownership model scales significantly better in larger organizations than a single, shared Ingress manifest that every team would otherwise need to coordinate changes through, reducing both coordination overhead and the blast radius of any single change.

Understanding that Ingress rules compose across multiple objects, rather than requiring one single monolithic manifest, is genuinely useful for correctly reading and reasoning about Ingress configuration in any moderately large, multi team cluster.
Path Based Routing and API Versioning
blocks.text: Path Based Routing and API Versioning

blocks.content: A genuinely common real world application of path based routing is API versioning, where slash v1 and slash v2 path prefixes route to two entirely separate backend Services, each running a different version of the same underlying API.

This lets an organization run both versions simultaneously during a migration period, giving existing clients time to move to the new version at their own pace while new clients are directed to slash v2 from the very beginning.

Once every client has migrated away from the older version, the slash v1 rule and its backing Service can simply be removed from the Ingress manifest, cleanly retiring the old version without touching the newer, still active v2 path at all.

This pattern is a genuinely practical, low risk way to manage API evolution over time, made possible entirely by the path based routing mechanism covered throughout this topic, without requiring any client side awareness of the underlying infrastructure change.
Path Matching Edge Cases Worth Knowing
blocks.text: Path Matching Edge Cases Worth Knowing

blocks.content: A path prefix of exactly slash matches every single request regardless of its actual path, which is why it is commonly used specifically as a catch all rule, but also why placing it carelessly among more specific rules can cause unintended shadowing.

Trailing slashes in a request path, such as slash api versus slash api slash, are typically treated as equivalent by most Ingress controller implementations under Prefix matching, though this exact behavior is worth confirming for controllers with unusually strict path handling.

Case sensitivity in path matching also varies by controller implementation, with most treating paths as case sensitive by default, meaning slash API and slash api could resolve to entirely different rules unless deliberately normalized beforehand.

None of these edge cases are common sources of real production problems, but knowing they exist helps explain occasional, otherwise puzzling routing behavior encountered while testing a new or unfamiliar Ingress controller implementation.
Path Based Routing for Static Assets
blocks.text: Path Based Routing for Static Assets

blocks.content: A common, practical pattern separates dynamic application traffic from static asset traffic, routing a path prefix such as slash static or slash assets to a dedicated, lightweight Service optimized specifically for serving unchanging files efficiently.

This separation lets the static asset Service be scaled, cached, and optimized entirely independently of the main application logic, without requiring any change to how the application itself serves or references those assets internally.

Some teams route static asset paths to an entirely different kind of backend altogether, such as a Service backed by object storage rather than an ordinary application Pod, using path based routing as the seam that makes this substitution invisible to the end user.

This pattern is a genuinely good illustration of path based routing's real power: it is not just about splitting one API from another, but about splitting any two logically distinct pieces of a single, cohesive user facing application.
Debugging a Path Based Routing Mismatch
blocks.text: Debugging a Path Based Routing Mismatch

blocks.content: When a specific path unexpectedly routes to the wrong backend, the first step is listing every Ingress object in the relevant namespace, since the rule causing the unexpected behavior may live in a manifest entirely separate from the one under active investigation.

The second step is checking the exact pathType and path value of every candidate rule for overlap, since a broader Prefix rule elsewhere in the same or a different Ingress object can silently intercept traffic intended for a more specific one.

The third step is testing directly with curl, exactly as covered earlier in this topic, isolating the Ingress controller's actual routing decision from any separate, unrelated application level behavior that might otherwise be mistakenly blamed.

Working through these three checks methodically, rather than guessing, resolves the overwhelming majority of path based routing mismatches quickly, and it is a habit directly worth carrying into the very next topic covering host based routing as well.

Testing Path Based Routing Locally

Before relying on real, public DNS, path based routing behavior can be tested directly against the Ingress controller's own external IP address using curl with an explicit Host header, confirming the routing logic works correctly before any DNS record even exists.

This local testing technique isolates the Ingress routing logic itself from any separate DNS related issues, letting an engineer confirm the manifest is correct independently of whether public DNS has been configured and propagated yet.

Running this kind of test as a standard step immediately after applying any new or modified Ingress manifest catches routing mistakes early, before real user traffic or automated monitoring has a chance to surface them instead.

This habit mirrors the layered debugging approach already established throughout the Services module: verify each piece of the chain independently, rather than only testing the fully assembled, end to end path all at once.
curl -H "Host: example.com" http://<ingress-external-ip>/api/users
Best Practices for Path Based Routing
blocks.text: Best Practices for Path Based Routing

blocks.content: Keep path prefixes short, predictable, and aligned with how the backend team already thinks about their own application's URL structure, avoiding surprising or deeply nested prefixes that complicate both routing and rewrite configuration.

Use the rewrite target annotation deliberately and document it clearly in the manifest, since an unexpected rewrite behavior is a common, hard to diagnose source of confusing 404 errors reported by backend teams unfamiliar with the Ingress layer.

Test routing changes with a direct curl request against the Ingress controller's address before relying on DNS propagation, catching manifest mistakes minutes rather than potentially hours after a change is applied.

Order and structure Ingress rules from most specific path to least specific path within any single manifest, rather than relying solely on implicit controller behavior to resolve overlapping prefixes correctly.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Path based routing turns the abstract promise of HTTP aware routing into a concrete, working mechanism: one hostname, many paths, each path directed to its own independently owned and independently scaled backend Service.

The prefix matching behavior, and the optional rewrite target annotation that strips that prefix before forwarding, are the two details that most directly determine whether a given manifest behaves exactly as intended in practice.

The next topic, Host Based Routing, covers the second of the two core mechanisms, splitting traffic by domain name rather than by path, and the two together form the complete routing vocabulary this entire module has been building toward.
Keep the curl with an explicit Host header testing technique in mind. It is the fastest, most reliable way to validate any Ingress routing change before real traffic or real DNS is ever involved.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: path prefixes are a design decision made once but lived with for a long time, so choosing them thoughtfully at the start pays off well beyond the initial setup effort.

Carry the three step debugging habit, list rules, compare paths, test with curl, directly into the next topic, since host based routing shares the exact same debugging shape with a hostname substituted for a path.
Path based routing is now fully covered; host based routing, its direct complement, follows immediately next.

blocks.title: Path Based Routing In Full
points: Path based routing directs requests to different backend Services based on URL path, using pathType Prefix or Exact to control exactly how that path is matched.
The Ingress controller applies the most specific matching path when rules overlap, though explicit rule ordering remains the safer, more predictable practice.
A rewrite target annotation can strip the matched path prefix before forwarding, letting backend applications remain unaware of the external path used to route to them.
Rules for the same host compose cleanly across multiple, independently owned Ingress objects, supporting decentralized ownership in larger organizations.
Host Based Routing, covered next, completes the routing vocabulary by splitting traffic by domain name rather than by path.
